title: 2 Chronicles 21:1–7
context: Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat begins his reign over Judah by killing his brothers, a deed recorded only in Chronicles. Married to Ahab’s daughter, he walks in the ways of Israel’s kings. Yet the LORD will not destroy David’s house, because of his covenant and his promise of a lamp. The parallel is 2 Kings 8:16–19, and the covenant promise is treated in the notes on 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Chronicles 17. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about a king’s grave sin and God’s faithfulness to his promise.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city; and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat dies and is buried in David’s city, and his son Jehoram reigns in his place. The parallel account begins at 2 Kings 8:16.

Arminian readers see a new king inheriting a godly father’s example and a real choice about whether to follow it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jehoshaphat’s reign had been largely commended in Chronicles. His son will take a very different path.

Reformed readers see the succession unfolding under God’s rule. Both traditions read this as shared ground about a transition that sets up the contrast between father and son.

verses.text: He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoram has six brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat, named here. This list does not appear in 2 Kings.

Arminian readers see the narrator naming the brothers individually before recording what happens to them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles here calls Jehoshaphat king of Israel, a usage it sometimes applies to Judah’s kings; the text does not explain it.

Reformed readers see each life valued in the record. Both traditions read this as shared ground and honor the named brothers as persons.

verses.text: Their father gave them great gifts of silver, of gold, and of precious things, with fortified cities in Judah; but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat gives his other sons generous gifts and fortified cities, but gives the kingdom to Jehoram as firstborn. He provides for all his sons.

Arminian readers see a father acting fairly and openly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The arrangement seems meant to secure peace in the royal family while preserving the firstborn’s right, though the text gives no motive.

Reformed readers see a wise provision that Jehoram will betray. Both traditions read this as shared ground about Jehoshaphat’s care for his family.

verses.text: Now when Jehoram had risen up over the kingdom of his father, and had strengthened himself, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Once established, Jehoram kills all his brothers with the sword, and some of Israel’s princes. The narrator reports this murder plainly.

Arminian readers see a grievous, deliberate choice for which Jehoram is fully responsible.
verses.reformedNotes:
This act is recorded only in Chronicles and is not explained. It will be named again in Elijah’s letter (21:13).

Reformed readers see the depth of sin in seizing security through bloodshed. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground and do not elaborate on it.

verses.text: Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoram is thirty-two when he begins to reign, and he reigns eight years in Jerusalem. The figures match 2 Kings 8:17.

Arminian readers see a reign whose length is recorded before its character is assessed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The same regnal figures are repeated at 21:20, framing the account of his reign.

Reformed readers see God measuring the days of kings. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, a standard regnal notice, and do not press it for chronological conclusions.

verses.text: He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did Ahab’s house, for he had Ahab’s daughter as his wife. He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoram walks in the way of Israel’s kings, like Ahab’s house, for he has married Ahab’s daughter, and he does evil. The verse closely follows 2 Kings 8:18.

Arminian readers see family alliance shaping a king’s free choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
The marriage alliance between Judah and Ahab’s house brings Ahab’s ways into Judah.

Reformed readers see the corrupting power of ungodly alliances. Both traditions read this as shared ground, holding Jehoram responsible for walking in that way.

verses.text: However the LORD would not destroy David’s house, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and as he promised to give a lamp to him and to his children always.
verses.arminianNotes:
Yet the LORD will not destroy David’s house because of his covenant with David and his promise to give him and his children a lamp always. Mercy rests on promise.

Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness despite the king’s unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Kings 8:19 says the LORD would not destroy Judah for David’s sake; Chronicles speaks of David’s house and the covenant.

Reformed readers see the promise of 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Chronicles 17 upheld. Both traditions read this as shared ground, as those notes explain.
